opus-5.5.text:
I think it's honestly a very good time, maybe one of the best, but the opportunities look different from a few years ago.

When I started, a lot of the low-hanging fruit was about making the model work at all: scaling, getting pretraining right, figuring out post-training. Those problems are still important, but they've become very industrialized. They need huge compute and big teams, so a young person's marginal contribution there is harder to see. That's not a reason to avoid it. Being inside a strong team and seeing how frontier systems are built is an incredible education. But you should be clear-eyed about it.

Where I think younger people have a real edge is in the questions that aren't well-defined yet. What should these models actually do in the world? How do you evaluate an agent working over hours or days? How do you build environments, tasks, and feedback that teach something useful? What does a product look like when the underlying capability changes every six months? These are questions where experience doesn't help much, and sometimes it even hurts, because people carry assumptions from the previous era. Someone who grew up with these models and uses them every day often has better intuition about what's possible.

My general advice is a few things. First, pick problems where, if the models keep getting better, your work becomes more valuable, not obsolete. A lot of clever engineering just gets washed away by the next model. Ask yourself whether you're betting with the trend or against it. Second, get close to the real thing. Use the models a lot, build with them, and run your own experiments, even small ones. Taste comes from contact, not from reading papers. Third, don't over-optimize for the prestige path. The field moves so fast that the "right" lab or the "right" topic two years ago may not be right now. What compounds is your ability to learn quickly and to judge what matters.

And maybe one more thing: think about what you find meaningful, not only what's hot. AI touches basically everything now, including science, education, and how people work. If you combine a deep understanding of the models with a real domain you care about, I think that's where a lot of the most interesting opportunities will come from in the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining and post-training have become industrialized, requiring huge compute and teams, which makes young entrants’ marginal contribution harder to see.

r002.rationale: It identifies science as a domain for interesting AI opportunities, but does not suggest those opportunities are more untapped than working purely on language models.

r003.rationale: It says younger people have an edge in questions that are not yet well-defined and advises against optimizing for what is currently prestigious or hot.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the opportunity is enormous, but it looks different from what it looked like for my generation, and that difference matters a lot for how you should choose.

When I started doing research, the game was mostly about ideas. You could be a PhD student with a handful of GPUs, come up with something like chain-of-thought or a new way to let a model use tools, and that idea alone could move the field. The barrier to entry was low and the bottleneck was imagination. A lot of the first half of AI, if you want to call it that, was about finding the right methods, and methods are something a smart person in a small lab can discover.

Now the methods are largely in place. Scaling works, reasoning with reinforcement learning works, agents work. So the frontier has shifted from "what is the right algorithm" to "what is the right problem, the right environment, the right way to measure." That is actually good news for younger people, because it means the most valuable work is no longer concentrated inside a few labs with the biggest compute. Defining what intelligence should be doing in the real world, building the tasks and feedback loops that teach a model to do it, understanding where models still fail and why, those are questions where a fresh perspective is an advantage rather than a handicap.

So my practical advice would be three things. First, don't try to compete on the thing that is already saturated. Training a slightly better base model is a race with very few winners and it is mostly decided by capital. Second, pick a domain you actually care about and go deep into it, whether that is science, software, healthcare, education, whatever. The people who will create the most value in the next decade are the ones who understand both how models work and what a real field actually needs, and that combination is rarer than it sounds. Third, develop taste. By that I mean the ability to look at a problem and judge whether it is important, whether it is tractable now, and whether solving it changes anything downstream. Taste comes from reading widely, building things end to end, and being honest with yourself when something doesn't work.

And I would say, don't be too anxious about timing. Every generation feels like the big discoveries already happened before they arrived. The people who worked on neural networks in the 2000s felt that way about the 1980s, and look how that turned out. The field is still very young. If anything, the gap between what models can do and what the world has actually absorbed is widening, and that gap is where the opportunities are. You just have to be willing to go stand in it.

r001.rationale: The response says training a slightly better base model is already saturated and largely decided by capital, so it is not an untapped opportunity for new entrants.

r002.rationale: It recommends going deep in domains including science, but does not clearly say that applying AI to scientific problems offers more untapped opportunity than working purely on language models.

r003.rationale: It advises younger people not to compete in the saturated race and instead to pursue meaningful domain problems where fresh perspectives can help.

astra-6.text:
I think there are still a lot of opportunities, but I would be careful about choosing a direction just because it looks promising today. If you’re younger than me, you have more time to explore, and the landscape may change several times before you settle on what you want to do.

One useful distinction is between what AI can do and what people can actually use it to accomplish. A model can perform well on a benchmark, but turning that capability into something that reliably solves a real problem takes a lot of work. You need to understand the problem, figure out how to evaluate success, and learn where the system breaks. That creates opportunities for people with very different backgrounds.

So I’d encourage someone to find a problem they care about and try to build something for it. Working on a concrete problem gives you much better feedback than trying to predict which area will be hottest in three years. You may discover that the bottleneck is a fundamental research question, or you may discover that existing models are already good enough and the missing piece is how to use them.

And I wouldn’t confuse being early with being prepared. You don’t have to have started before everyone else. Building good judgment, learning how to ask questions, and getting comfortable testing your ideas are things that keep paying off even as the technology changes.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes model benchmark performance from practical use, but does not say that work focused purely on language models is no longer largely untapped.

r002.rationale: It mentions concrete problems and possible fundamental research, but does not specifically compare scientific problems with language-model work or say science offers more untapped opportunity.

r003.rationale: It advises trying a concrete problem rather than predicting the hottest area, but does not communicate that young people should pursue unexplored directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is still very large, but I wouldn’t choose a direction simply because it’s popular today. The field changes so quickly that if you spend all your time following what everyone else is doing, you may always be a little late.

For someone younger, I would focus on two things: building strong fundamentals and developing your own judgment. Fundamentals help you adapt when the technology changes. Judgment comes from actually trying things—building a system, watching where it fails, and asking why. Sometimes a small project teaches you more than reading many papers because you have to confront the gap between an idea and something that works.

There are opportunities both in improving models and in figuring out how to use them. You don’t necessarily need to train a larger model to make a meaningful contribution. You might find a task that current systems should be able to do, discover why they cannot do it reliably, and develop a better approach.

So I would encourage people to explore, but also to stay with a question long enough to understand it deeply. The important thing is to gradually find a problem where you have some insight of your own.

r001.rationale: The response says opportunities remain large and discusses improving models and using them, but does not judge whether language-model work is largely untapped.

r002.rationale: It does not mention applying AI to scientific problems or compare that with language-model work.

r003.rationale: It advises against choosing a direction only because it is popular and encourages finding a problem of personal insight, but does not clearly recommend pursuing unexplored directions.
